title: AI is not there yet for generating 3D models. Or is it?
author: Virtual_Wash8888
selftext:
For last couple of years I've been watching how generative AI evolves in the space of 3D Art.   
I've been working in gamedev as Environment Artist for a decade, so my interest has been mostly professional. I've always felt like "it's not there yet", meaning AI meshes could be suitable mostly as temporary blockouts or some inspiration.  
  
However, recently I've stumbled upon some nicely textured meshes, that have been made by AI, and decided to make a deeper dive into this subject.  
  
The result you can see at the screenshot.   
Made in Godot, in two evenings. Started as some tools testing, it ended up as a complete real time environment  
All the models and textures you see have been made completely by AI, with the exception of one tree, and some grass with terrain textures from Megascans. I haven't been manually touching the meshes, textures or UVs. My job was to approve concepts, models and to work on placement, composition and lighting. Basically I've been positioned as an Art Director with a team of 2D and 3D Artists  
  
*Workflow:*  
Claude Code orchestrates, GPT-6 generates 2D concepts, Meshy creates models  
I give a task to Fable, say "create old weathered fishing boat", it sends request to GPT-6/Codex, which generates 2D concept. As soon as it's done, Claude grabs the result, gives it to Meshy and tells it to create textured mesh in highest resolution and in desired polycount. After generation is finished, Meshy pushes it to Godot through its Bridge, where Claude catches it and organizes everything for me  
  
*Tools:*  
Meshy, Godot, Claude Code as an orchestrator, Codex for image generation  
No external post processing applied to the final image, raw from the engine  
  
*Tech stuff*:  
From the camera view - 2,765,169 triangles, 115 draw calls and 2.2GB VRAM - quite good for AI generated stuff without LODs, batching, etc  
It ran at 60 fps in 2560x1440 on RTX2060 laptop before I maxed everything out and went all in with SDFGI, TAA, shadows, heavy alphas, etc for final image. I'm sure with some optimization tweaks it will run at 60fps while keeping \~80-85% of the look

*Time:*  
Two evenings, roughly 8-10 hours. Could've been done much faster if I'd had a concept in mind prior to starting. Most of the time went into iterating on composition, not into production

comments.body: i think you've solved Modelling. Can you try to solve animating now? We need a master like you to help.

comments.author: EchoingAngel
comments.body: There's two major trade offs, at least outside of nanite: you either have very few, great looking models, or you have more, messy models. As a factory game, I have to go with "more", but that means restricting how close players can get to the surfaces, as they look bad (and I'm on Unity)

comments.author: imnotabot303
comments.body:
AI 3D gen is currently at the level of photogrammetry.

Some of them can create good models but they are going to need cleanup and optimisation if you want to use them for anything more than a static mesh in a render.

There's also things that it will struggle with for quite a while imo, such as complex hard surface models that need to be animated. Like a complex robot for example.

comments.author: delusion54
comments.body:
Why meshy? Also are you using a custom skill? I think I overcomplicated my [SKILL.md](http://SKILL.md) and takes too long but results are decent for AI work. I am specifically troubled by 3d creatures models, because of the troubles hands and join transitions produce.   
  
For context, my setup is codex, higgsfield blender mcp, blender, godot. I usually feed an image and ideally sprites from a video generated based on my initially approved generated image.

If you have any advice much appreciated.
